title: Limits of Trigonometric Functions
notes: **Standard trigonometric limits:** These are essential tools for evaluating limits involving trigonometric functions.
**Primary limit:** lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1 (where x is in radians).
**Tangent limit:** lim(x→0) tan(x)/x = 1 (follows from sin/cos limits).
**Prerequisites:** Basic trigonometry formulas from class 10 plus these limit-specific formulas.
**Key technique:** Use trigonometric identities to transform expressions into standard forms.
**Important:** All trigonometric limits assume x is measured in radians, not degrees.
**Applications:** These limits are fundamental for deriving derivatives of trigonometric functions.
confusion: The limit sin(x)/x → 1 only holds when x → 0, not for other values of x.
Radians vs degrees: if x is in degrees, lim(x→0) sin(x)/x ≠ 1 — must convert to radians.
Don't confuse lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1 with lim(x→0) cos(x)/x (which does not exist).
The limit (1-cos x)/x → 0 is different from (1-cos x)/x² → 1/2 (a related but different limit).
These limits are indeterminate forms 0/0 but resolve to specific values through geometric proof.
practice: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin(5x)/x using the standard limit sin(x)/x → 1.
Find lim(x→0) (1-cos(3x))/x using trigonometric identities and standard limits.
Evaluate lim(x→0) tan(2x)/x using the standard tangent limit.
Find lim(x→0) sin(3x)/sin(2x) by rewriting in terms of standard limits.
Evaluate lim(x→0) (sin x - x cos x)/x³ using appropriate trigonometric manipulations.
universalFacts: Trigonometric limits are proven using the squeeze theorem and geometric arguments with the unit circle.
These limits are essential for deriving the derivatives of sin(x) and cos(x) in calculus.
The radian measure is natural for calculus because it makes these limits work cleanly.
Similar limit techniques apply to inverse trigonometric functions.
These limits appear in physics when analyzing oscillatory motion and wave phenomena.
